era_visual_canon.clothing: Mining-era miners and mill workers: sweat-stained cotton work shirts or sleeveless singlets, khaki or denim work trousers, heavy leather work boots, felt or wide-brimmed hats. They work in dust-coated clothes, generally without respiratory protection. Company managers, mines inspectors, doctors and officials: light wool or cotton suits, white shirts, ties, felt hats; in the field, khaki shirts with rolled sleeves. Women: simple cotton print dresses or skirts and blouses, cardigans, headscarves against dust and sun. Children: cotton shorts, short dresses and sandals, often barefoot on dusty ground. Later legal and activist scenes from the 1980s onward: contemporary business suits and outdoor casual wear appropriate to each decade.
era_visual_canon.technology: Mining era (1937-1966): mechanical ore crushing and fibre-milling plant with belt drives, hoppers and dust-extraction ducting added later; hand-held pneumatic rock drills; explosives; kerosene lamps; valve radios; manual typewriters, carbon-copy reports and paper files; wall-mounted or desk telephones and telegrams; black-and-white and early colour film photography. NO computers, NO digital displays, NO mobile phones, NO modern respirators or disposable dust masks, NO plastic safety signage. Post-closure era: period-appropriate technology only for each decade; a 2020s scene may show modern devices, but never in mining-era scenes.
era_visual_canon.vehicles_machinery: Round-fendered 1930s-1950s utility vehicles and flatbed or tip trucks hauling ore and dumping tailings on red dirt roads. Ore trucks and mine haulage equipment at the gorge workings. Small twin-engine piston propeller aircraft landing on a dusty airstrip surfaced with tailings. Mill machinery: crushers, conveyor belts, rotating screens and bagging plant for asbestos fibre. Post-closure: demolition machinery and later 4WD vehicles stopped at permanent road barricades.
era_visual_canon.interiors: Small company houses of corrugated iron and timber lined with asbestos-cement fibro sheeting. Linoleum or bare timber floors, enamel kitchenware, ice chests or early refrigerators, simple timber furniture, dust settling on every surface. Small rural hospital with iron-framed beds and basic obstetric equipment. Plain government and company offices with timber desks, filing cabinets and typewriters. Later: a modern interview setting surrounded by sepia family photographs.
era_visual_canon.forbidden_anachronisms: In mining-era scenes (1937-1966): no modern P2/N95 respirators, hazmat suits, high-visibility vests or hard hats with modern logos; no sealed bitumen roads with painted lines; no modern 4WD SUVs or modern mining haul trucks; no jet aircraft at the airstrip; no plastic road barriers or printed asbestos warning signs; no smartphones, digital cameras or LED lighting; no solar panels or satellite dishes on houses.
era_visual_canon.materials_textures: Corrugated sheet iron, timber framing and asbestos-cement fibro sheeting on dwellings. Loose, crumbly, fibrous asbestos mill tailings spread and compacted as the surface of roads, yards, the airstrip, schoolyard and public spaces. Raw asbestos fibre that frays into soft threads and sheds fine powdery dust when touched. Dry powdery earth. Water-deposited fibrous sediment in creek beds, rock pools and floodplains.
era_visual_canon.color_palette: Exterior intense red earth and rust-red dust, blue-grey tailings surfaces (INFERENCE from the mineral name 'blue asbestos'), weathered silver-grey corrugated iron, pale grey-white fibro walls and a pale beige-grey dust haze hanging around the mill; interior colours not documented.
era_visual_canon.scale_dimensions: Official Wittenoom Asbestos Management Area of 46,840 hectares. More than three million tonnes of tailings left behind. About 150,000 tonnes of commercial asbestos produced by three mines. Contamination extends along creeks to the Fortescue River catchment. Dwellings likely small single-storey houses (INFERENCE, not documented).
era_visual_canon.distinctive_features: A remote red-earth Pilbara town whose roads, yards, schoolyard and airstrip were literally paved with blue asbestos mill tailings, with a mill shrouded in dust clouds during operation. Today it is a vast erased zone sealed by permanent barricades.
era_visual_canon.demographics: The mining-era workforce was male miners and mill workers: Australian union members, post-war European displaced persons assigned 1948-1951, CSR-recruited Europeans from 1950, and Spanish migrants arriving through the 1958 Spain-Australia agreement. Families included young Spanish wives and children born or raised in the town. Workers wore dust-covered work clothes; children played among tailings. The land belongs to Banjima Aboriginal traditional owners, documented as elders and activists in the 2020s. Australian mines inspectors, public health doctors and company managers appear as visitors and officials.
era_visual_canon.visual_reference_availability: No [VISUAL] research block was supplied; no photographs, plans or footage were reviewed. Every place and object detail is TEXT-SOURCED. Migrant oral testimony supplies the red earth, pervasive dust, corrugated-iron, timber and fibro housing, small propeller plane and fraying asbestos. The 1957 Board of Reference report supplies the mill dust cloud and dust-covered workers. A former worker's testimony places tailings in yards, accesses, schools, kindergarten and churches. Environmental reports document fibre deposits in creeks, pools and floodplains. Official descriptions document the permanent access barricades. Family photographs are said to exist (bandaged-foot portrait, baptism photo dated 1963-07-07, sepia photos at an interview), but they were not viewed. The blue-grey tailings colour is INFERENCE from the mineral name. Building size and interior colours are INFERENCE or undocumented. Demographic origins come from the written record, not photographs.

condition_evolution.at_event: An operating company mining town (1937-1966). The mill runs under a thick suspended dust cloud while trucks haul ore and dump tailings. Corrugated-iron and fibro houses are inhabited. Freshly spread tailings surface the roads, yards, schoolyard and dusty airstrip. Workers are coated in dust and children play with loose fibre.
condition_evolution.later: After the December 1966 closure, the town was progressively shrunk from 1978. Buildings were demolished and the school, nursing post and police station closed between 1986 and 1992, and the airport closed in 1993. Power was cut in 2006 and the town was removed from maps and signs in 2007. The last residents left by 2022-2023 and the remaining structures were demolished. Eroding tailings dumps now wash fibre into creeks toward the Fortescue, and permanent barricades block every access road.

periods.clothing: Prospectors and early miners in khaki shirts, moleskin or denim trousers, felt bush hats and leather boots. Wartime officials in wool suits and ties.
periods.technology: Hand tools, rock drills, explosives, rudimentary crushing plant, kerosene lamps, valve radios, typewritten mines reports, telegrams.
periods.vehicles_machinery: 1930s round-fendered trucks and utes on unsealed red tracks, pack loads and small early crushing machinery at the gorges.
periods.interiors: Rough camp huts and corrugated-iron shelters, canvas tents, bare timber tables, kerosene lighting.

periods.clothing: Male workers, including post-war European and Spanish migrants, in dust-coated cotton work shirts, singlets, work trousers and boots. Migrant women in cotton print dresses and headscarves. Children in shorts and simple dresses, often barefoot. Managers and doctors in light suits.
periods.technology: Expanded fibre mill with belts, screens and later dust-reduction ducting; pneumatic drills; landline telephones; manual typewriters; film cameras; valve radios. No digital technology.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Late-1940s to early-1960s trucks and tip trucks spreading tailings, company utes, small twin-engine propeller aircraft at a dusty airstrip.
periods.interiors: Corrugated-iron and fibro company houses with linoleum floors, enamel kitchenware and early refrigerators. Small town hospital ward. School classrooms with timber desks.

periods.clothing: Remaining residents and former workers in late-1960s to 1980s casual wear. Lawyers, judges and politicians in 1980s suits. Ageing ex-workers and widows in plain clothes at courts and meetings.
periods.technology: Landline phones, typewriters giving way to early office computers in city offices only, analogue television news cameras, film photography.
periods.vehicles_machinery: 1970s-1980s sedans and 4WDs on degraded roads, demolition equipment removing town buildings, airstrip closing.
periods.interiors: Shrinking town with closing school, nursing post and police station. City courtrooms and parliamentary hearing rooms with timber panelling.

periods.clothing: Contemporary outdoor workwear, business suits for officials and lawyers, casual clothing for Banjima community members and activists.
periods.technology: Contemporary devices permitted only in these scenes: digital cameras, laptops at press conferences, printed warning signage.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Modern 4WD vehicles halted at permanent barricades, earthmoving equipment for final demolitions.
periods.interiors: Government offices, law firm meeting rooms, interview rooms with family photographs.

people_groups.who: Australian prospectors and early mine owners and managers who opened the blue asbestos workings and later sold their interests to ABA/CSR.
people_groups.where_when: Yampire and Wittenoom Gorges in the Hamersley Ranges, 1937-1943.
people_groups.appearance: White European-descended Australian men, sun-weathered and wiry from outback fieldwork, with short-cropped hair.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Khaki or faded cotton work shirts with rolled sleeves, moleskin or denim trousers, leather boots and wide-brimmed felt bush hats, suited to dry desert heat.

people_groups.who: Male asbestos miners, mill fitters and labourers, including Australian AWU members, post-war European displaced persons, CSR-recruited Europeans and later Spanish migrants.
people_groups.where_when: Wittenoom mines and mill, 1937-1966; surviving former workers reappear in compensation claims and court cases from 1979 to 1989.
people_groups.appearance: Mostly white Australian and European men with sunburned skin, lean muscular labouring builds, short hair and faces, hair and arms coated in fine dust.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Sweat-stained cotton work shirts or singlets, heavy work trousers, leather boots and felt hats, with no respiratory protection.
Dust-covered singlets or short-sleeved work shirts, shorts or work trousers, leather boots, short-back-and-sides haircuts, occasionally a cloth hat, and generally no respirators.
Ageing former workers in plain button-up shirts, cardigans or modest suits at hearings, with greying hair and some visibly ill.

people_groups.who: Spanish migrant miners, their wives and children from Madrid and other parts of Spain, who arrived under the 1958 Spain-Australia migration agreement.
people_groups.where_when: Ship voyage via Suez and arrival at Wittenoom in 1962, residence 1962-1964, returns to Madrid in 1966 and 1971; children later reappear as adults in 1985 and in later interviews alongside their elderly mothers.
people_groups.appearance: Spanish Mediterranean people with light-olive to olive skin, dark brown or black hair and dark eyes; the men have slim working builds and the women are young.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Men in dusty work shirts and trousers or their best suits for photos; women in cotton print shirtwaist dresses, cardigans and headscarves, with set or permed hair; children in shorts, short dresses and sandals or barefoot.
Modest late-1960s Spanish urban clothing on return to Madrid: men in jackets and slacks, women in knee-length dresses and coats, children in school clothes.
Adult children in mid-1980s casual wear such as jackets, jeans and open-collar shirts; parents in conservative middle-aged clothing with greying hair.
Elderly women in plain cardigans and blouses at interviews; middle-aged children in contemporary smart-casual media-professional attire.

people_groups.who: Western Australian Mines Department officials, including the Inspector of Mines, the Deputy State Mining Engineer and health inspectors who reported on the dust.
people_groups.where_when: Visiting the Wittenoom mine and mill and writing reports from state offices, 1944-1966.
people_groups.appearance: White Anglo-Australian men of mature age with office or field complexions and short neat hair.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Light wool or cotton suits with ties and felt hats in offices; khaki shirts, trousers and boots on site inspections.

people_groups.who: Australian public health doctors, the Public Health Commissioner and an industrial hygienist who warned about asbestos dust and diagnosed disease.
people_groups.where_when: Wittenoom and state health offices, 1948-1951, 1960-1968, including a 1965 schoolyard reprimand and a 1966 machinery inspection.
people_groups.appearance: White Anglo-Australian men with professional builds and short neatly combed hair.

clothing_by_period.clothing: White shirts, ties and light suits or white coats, felt hats outdoors, and leather shoes dusted red on site visits.

people_groups.who: Managers of ABA and executives and chairmen of the Australian sugar-industry company CSR that ran the mine.
people_groups.where_when: Wittenoom site management and Sydney corporate offices, 1943-1966, including a 1949 employer representative and the 1966 closure announcement.
people_groups.appearance: White Anglo-Australian middle-aged men of business-class build with neatly groomed short hair.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Dark or light business suits, crisp shirts and ties, polished shoes and felt hats; site managers in short-sleeved shirts and slacks.

people_groups.who: Australian AWU union officials and members of the industrial arbitration court and Board of Reference who negotiated and assessed dust allowances.
people_groups.where_when: Arbitration hearings and the Wittenoom mill, 1946-1959, including the 1957 Board of Reference inspection.
people_groups.appearance: White Anglo-Australian men: union officials with working-class builds, arbitrators of mature age with professional bearing.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Union officials in open-collar shirts and plain jackets; arbitrators and board members in suits and ties, removing jackets in the mill heat.

people_groups.who: Australian federal and Western Australian politicians and government agencies, including a Prime Minister, Lands Ministers, parliamentary inquiry chairs and state agencies.
people_groups.where_when: Canberra and Perth offices and parliament, 1947, 1978-1994 and 2006-2026.
people_groups.appearance: Australian adults of the governing class, predominantly white Anglo-Australian in earlier decades.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Dark double- or single-breasted wool suits, white shirts, ties and felt hats.
Late-1970s to early-1990s business suits with wide or patterned ties and side-parted hair.
Contemporary tailored business suits or smart-casual attire at press conferences.

people_groups.who: The last residents who stayed in the shrinking town, including members of the local Wittenoom steering committee.
people_groups.where_when: Wittenoom township from the 1978 reduction policy to the departure of the last residents in 2022-2023.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Practical outback casual wear of each decade: cotton shirts, shorts or jeans, boots or thongs, and broad-brimmed hats against the sun.

people_groups.who: Banjima Aboriginal traditional owners of the Pilbara land, including elders, activists and BNTAC board members.
people_groups.where_when: Wittenoom and Banjima country, 2023-2026, including the UN rapporteur meeting and the federal court action.
people_groups.appearance: Aboriginal Australian people with medium to dark brown skin and dark wavy or curly hair, greying in elders, with builds shaped by outdoor life.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Contemporary casual outdoor clothing such as cotton shirts, work trousers or jeans and broad-brimmed hats, with collared shirts or jackets for legal and media appearances.
